extracted.intended_audience: federal district court judges and court staff (case managers) handling patent litigation; patent litigators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for early-stage patent case management: standing and declaratory-judgment jurisdiction, joinder and defendant/party requirements, and pleading standards for infringement and related claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonexclusive (bare) licensee lacks standing
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonexclusive (or “bare”) licensee suffers no legal injury from infringement and therefore lacks standing to sue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Intellectual Prop. Dev., Inc. v. TCI Cablevision of Cal., Inc., 248 F.3d 1333, 1345 (Fed. Cir. 2001). Nonexclusive licensees generally cannot invoke the patentee’s rights because they do not suffer the legal injury that confers standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment or exclusive license conveying substantially all rights confers right to sue
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment of a patent, or an exclusive license of a patent that conveys substantially all patent rights, conveys to the assignee or licensee the right to sue for present and future infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent holder cannot confer a right to sue separate from conveying a proprietary interest. To have standing to sue, a party must be an exclusive licensee or assignee of all substantial rights (see Propat Int’l, 473 F.3d at 1189). The right to sue for prior infringement is not transferred unless the assignment agreement manifests an intent to transfer that right; courts analyze assignments under state contract law and do not require a particular formula of words (see Minco Inc. v. Combustion Eng’g, 95 F.3d 1109, 1117 (Fed. Cir. 1996)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenant not to sue or binding representation can moot controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: A party’s issuance of a covenant not to sue or similarly binding representation that it will not resume enforcement against the declaratory judgment plaintiff can render the case moot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 133 S. Ct. 721, 725 (2013) (trademark); Organic Seed Growers & Trade Ass’n v. Monsanto Co., 718 F.3d 1350 (Fed. Cir. 2013) (applying Nike). Timing is key: covenants given prior to consideration or resolution of the underlying infringement claim may be effective (Benitec Austl., Ltd. v. Nucleonics, Inc., 495 F.3d 1340, 1347), but a covenant given after resolution of infringement claims will not result in dismissal (Fort James Corp. v. Solo Cup Co., 412 F.3d 1340, 1348). Courts examine whether the representation is judicially binding and whether it assures that enforcement efforts will not resume (see Danisco U.S. Inc. v. Novozymes A/S).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal for lack of standing usually without prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: If a case must be dismissed for lack of standing, it should ordinarily be dismissed without prejudice so the plaintiff may correct the defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Propat Int’l Corp. v. RPost US, Inc., 473 F.3d 1187, 1194 (Fed. Cir. 2007). A dismissal without prejudice permits correction of standing defects (e.g., joining co-owners). Where the basis for dismissal cannot be rectified (for example, where a covenant not to sue moots the controversy), dismissal should be with prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaratory-judgment plaintiff: actual controversy standard (MedImmune)
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court has subject-matter jurisdiction over a patent declaratory-judgment action when an 'actual controversy' exists between the parties—facts showing a substantial controversy of sufficient immediacy and reality to warrant a conclusive declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory basis: 28 U.S.C. § 2201(a). Supreme Court: MedImmune, Inc. v. Genentech, Inc., 549 U.S. 118 (2007) (rejecting 'reasonable apprehension of suit' test and requiring a definite, concrete dispute). Federal Circuit interpretation: jurisdiction exists when 'a patentee asserts rights under a patent based on certain identified ongoing or planned activity of another party, and where that party contends that it has the right to engage in the accused activity without license' (SanDisk Corp. v. STMicroelectronics, Inc., 480 F.3d 1372, 1381). There is no safe-harbor form of notice: attempts to avoid 'magic words' do not necessarily prevent jurisdiction (Hewlett-Packard Co. v. Acceleron LLC, 587 F.3d 1358, 1362).

rubrics_metrics.name: Planned or future activity can support declaratory-judgment jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Planned future commercial activity can be sufficiently imminent to create a justiciable controversy for a declaratory judgment even if the commercial launch is substantially in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arkema Inc. v. Honeywell Int’l Inc., 706 F.3d 1351 (Fed. Cir. 2013): Federal Circuit held that long-term supply contracts and a U.S. commercial launch at least a year away nevertheless presented a present position of committing to contracts that could expose the party to liability, and thus the dispute had sufficient immediacy and reality. Supplier-vs-patentee suits are another category where DJ jurisdiction commonly arises (e.g., supplier suing when patentee sues or threatens supplier’s customers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant’s declaratory-judgment counterclaims not mooted by plaintiff’s dismissal/affirmance
rubrics_metrics.description: An accused infringer’s declaratory-judgment counterclaim of invalidity is not necessarily mooted by dismissal or appellate affirmation of noninfringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cardinal Chem. Co. v. Morton Int’l, Inc., 508 U.S. 83, 98 (1993) held that appellate affirmation of noninfringement does not moot invalidity counterclaims because resolving patent validity is important to the public. However, district courts have discretion under the Declaratory Judgment Act to decline to resolve an invalidity claim after adjudication of noninfringement (MedImmune, 549 U.S. at 136).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignor estoppel and privity
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor who assigns patent rights is estopped from asserting invalidity as a defense or as the basis of a declaratory-judgment claim; those in privity with the assignor may also be estopped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrine sources: Pandrol USA, LP v. Airboss Ry. Prods., Inc., 424 F.3d 1161 (Fed. Cir. 2005); Diamond Sci. Co. v. Ambico, Inc., 848 F.2d 1220 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Assignor estoppel is an equitable doctrine concerned with balancing equities and functions as an affirmative defense, not a separate federal cause of action. Privity is determined by balance-of-equities factors and may consider (1) extent and nature of business relationships, (2) financial dealings such as indemnification agreements, and (3) whether the alleged infringer availed itself of the inventor’s knowledge and assistance (Intel Corp. v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 946 F.2d 821 (Fed. Cir. 1991); Checkpoint Sys. v. All-Tag Sec. S.A., 412 F.3d 1331 (Fed. Cir. 2005)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee in good standing can have actual controversy without breach
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent licensee who is performing under the license (e.g., paying royalties) may nonetheless present a controversy sufficient to support a declaratory-judgment action without first breaching or terminating the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court reversed prior rule in MedImmune, Inc. v. Genentech, Inc., 549 U.S. 118 (2007), holding a licensee need not break or terminate its license before seeking a DJ that the patent is invalid, unenforceable, or not infringed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee need not sue all accused infringers; direct infringers need not be joined
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent holder is not obligated to sue all accused infringers and may select among alleged infringers; direct infringers do not have to be parties in a suit against a contributory or induced infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Giese v. Pierce Chem. Co., 29 F. Supp. 2d 33 (D. Mass. 1998) and Refac Int’l, Ltd. v. IBM, 790 F.2d 79 (Fed. Cir. 1986). Joinder of direct infringers is not a prerequisite to suit against contributory infringers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder standards after In re EMC and the AIA §299
rubrics_metrics.description: Joinder of multiple accused infringers requires an 'actual link'—shared, overlapping facts that give rise to each cause of action; mere common infringement of the same patent is insufficient. The AIA §299 narrows joinder in patent cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re EMC Corp., 677 F.3d 1351 (Fed. Cir. 2012) requires a link between facts underlying each claim of infringement. AIA §299(a)(1) permits joinder only where (1) any right to relief is asserted against the parties jointly, severally, or in the alternative with respect to or arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions relating to the making, using, importing into the U.S., offering for sale, or selling of the same accused product or processes; and (2) common questions of fact will arise. §299(b) expressly states that common infringement of the same patent alone is not enough. §299(c) allows consent to joinder. District courts retain discretion to refuse joinder to avoid prejudice, delay, or unfairness; courts have severed defendants under §299 and have also consolidated pretrial proceedings (e.g., for claim construction) while preserving separate trials. Be alert to serially filed cases and potential abuse (e.g., filing to avoid deadlines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaratory-judgment defendants: necessary parties
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaratory-judgment action seeking to invalidate or render unenforceable a patent must name as defendants all parties holding an interest in the patent, although nonexclusive licensees are generally not necessary parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: In-Tech Mktg. Inc. v. Hasbro, Inc., 685 F. Supp. 436 (D.N.J. 1988) (licensor/exclusive licensee issues); Meese v. Eaton Mfg. Co., 35 F.R.D. 162 (N.D. Ohio 1964). Independent Wireless and older authority describe historical views, but courts often treat mere licensees as not indispensable; exclusive licensees may be necessary in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement pleading requirements and specificity (Form 18 vs Twombly/Iqbal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints should identify the asserted patents, state ownership of the patents, identify the accused infringers, provide a brief statement of alleged infringing acts, and, if applicable, state marking under §287. There is tension between historical Form 18 practice and the heightened pleading standards of Twombly/Iqbal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically notice pleading (Rule 8(a) and Form 18) produced sparse, conclusory patent complaints, sometimes omitting which claims or products were accused. Supreme Court decisions (Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007); Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)) require pleadings to state plausible claims with sufficient factual matter. The Federal Circuit has held Form 18 controlling for direct infringement in some cases (In re Bill of Lading, 681 F.3d 1323; McZeal v. Sprint Nextel Corp., 501 F.3d 1354), and held a complaint conforming to Form 18 may not need to identify a specific accused product (K-Tech, 714 F.3d 1277). District courts are split: some apply Twombly/Iqbal to patent complaints (Macronix Int’l Co. v. Spansion Inc., 4 F. Supp. 3d 797), others follow the Federal Circuit. On Dec 1, 2015, Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms (including Form 18) were abolished; Twombly/Iqbal pleading standards now govern patent complaints. For indirect infringement, courts generally require more detailed allegations (identity of underlying direct infringer and facts supporting specific-intent knowledge), and courts disagree on whether the filing of the complaint alone suffices to establish postsuit knowledge (compare Bascom Research LLC v. Facebook, Inc. and Mallinckrodt Inc. v. E-Z-EM Inc.). Some courts require identification of specific accused products; Rule 11(b)(3) permits allegations likely to have evidentiary support after discovery, but some courts hold Rule 11(b)(3) does not lower Rule 8(a) standards. Local rules (e.g., N.D. Cal. Patent L.R. 3-1) may require early disclosure of asserted claims and accused products, and amendment of those disclosures typically requires leave for good cause (see O2 Micro, Abbott Diabetes Care Inc. v. Roche Diagnostics Corp.).
